title: Text, date and title
short: Untitled in manuscript; first printed in 1920. The archive text is the three-stanza baiting sequence, omitting Clare's opening natural-history stanzas.
body: Clare left this poem untitled, so editors call it 'Badger' or '[The Badger]'. It was first published by Edmund Blunden and Alan Porter in Poems Chiefly from Manuscript (1920). The fuller manuscript version is a group of sonnet-length blocks in couplets (sixty-eight lines in five blocks in Brewer's description) that begins with the badger's habits and ends with a tame badger; anthologies, like this archive, often print only the central stanzas of the hunt and baiting. Modern editors such as Robinson and Powell generally place it among the Northborough poems of the mid-1830s, before Clare's admission to an asylum in 1837, so the archive's description of it as an asylum poem should be treated with caution. David Perkins discusses the group as 'badger sonnets'.

anchor: put a sack within the hole
title: Catching the badger
short: The hunters stop the earth with a sack and wait for the badger to return from foraging and run into it.
body: Badgers forage by night, so the men wait for the animal's return to its 'den' (its sett), having placed a sack in the entrance to trap it. 'Grunting' is accurate natural observation of the badger's noises. 'Bye' is Clare's spelling of 'by', and his unconventional spelling and punctuation are retained in many editions. The detail is plainly from a countryman's experience rather than literary convention.

anchor: The old fox hears the noise
title: Fox, poacher and hare
short: The night uproar disturbs the whole countryside: the fox drops its stolen goose, a poacher flees, a wounded hare runs past.
body: These lines widen the scene into a nocturnal panorama of rural life, and each figure is itself a predator or a victim: the fox with its goose, the poacher with his gun, the hare 'half wounded'. Clare's world is not idyllic; violence runs through all its levels. 'Buzzes bye' is an odd, vivid verb for the hare's rapid passage, suggesting a whirring sound or blur.

title: Forked stick
short: A cleft stick used to pin the badger by the neck so that it can be bagged.
body: The forked stick pins the animal to the ground without the hunter coming within reach of its strong bite. The men then 'clap the dogs', setting them on or encouraging them, and 'take him to the town', where the baiting becomes a public spectacle. The move from field to town shifts the poem from hunting to entertainment. The phrase 'bear him down' implies the animal's resistance even at capture.

title: Clap
short: Probably to set on or urge the dogs, perhaps by clapping hands or patting them; editors treat it as a dialect usage.
body: 'Clap' recurs in 'The dogs are clapt and urged to join the fray' (l. 19), where it is paired with 'urged', which suggests the sense of encouraging or setting on dogs with claps and shouts. Clare's vocabulary mixes standard English with East Midlands dialect, and editors such as Robinson and Powell gloss such words in their glossaries. The exact nuance is uncertain, but the sense of goading is clear from context.

title: Badger-baiting
short: Setting dogs on a captive animal for sport; Parliament outlawed animal baiting in 1835, though it long persisted.
body: Baiting (from Old Norse beita, 'to cause to bite') means setting dogs on a captive bull, bear or badger. It was a popular rural and urban entertainment, often accompanied by betting and drinking. The Cruelty to Animals Act of 1835 banned the baiting of animals in England and Wales, but enforcement was weak and badger-baiting continued illegally. Perkins places Clare's poem in this social history, noting that the 'savage amusements of the poor' were attacked by reformers while being part of village culture. Clare neither preaches nor approves; the moral judgement is carried by description.

title: The noisy streets
short: The baiting turns the town into chaos: pigs scatter, crowds shout down the streets as the badger runs and bites.
body: Pigs often roamed freely in town streets in the period, and the scattering hogs add a note of farce to the scene. The crowd's laughter and shouting contrast with the badger's single-minded fighting. The first stanza ends with the badger loose in the 'noisy streets', biting 'at all he meets', a reversal in which the hunted becomes the attacker. The 'noisy streets' mark the public, holiday character of the baiting.

title: Rebels
short: Mock-heroic: the crowd are cast as rebels routed by the badger as if by a lawful king or general.
body: Calling the townspeople 'rebels' inverts the moral order. The badger is treated as the rightful party, the crowd as insurgents whom he drives back 'to their very door'. The phrase belongs to a pattern of epic and military diction in the poem ('fray', 'foe', 'uproar') that gives the small animal heroic stature. Critics have read this as Clare's sympathy with the beleaguered creature, and sometimes, given Clare's own position, with the rural poor and outsiders.

title: 'The frequent stone'
short: A Latinate, poetic phrase meaning 'many stones' or 'stones again and again'; 'where eer' is 'wherever'.
body: The singular with 'frequent' (in the Latin sense of 'crowded, repeated') is an eighteenth-century poetic idiom, an instance of Clare's mixing of literary diction with plain speech. The next line, 'When badgers fight, then every one's a foe', is proverbial in shape: the badger is everyone's enemy, and everyone his. The stoning, too, shows the crowd's readiness to attack from a safe distance, where the dogs must fight at close quarters.

title: The badger's courage
short: The small, 'demure' badger beats bigger dogs; even the mastiff gives up and the bulldog 'waxes cold'.
body: These lines are the poem's celebration of the badger's courage. 'Demure' (quiet, modest) is an unexpected word for a fighter, stressing that the animal is not naturally aggressive. The 'heavy mastiff' gives up and licks its feet; the bulldog, bred for baiting and famous for never letting go, 'knows his match and waxes cold' (grows faint-hearted). 'The badger grins and never leaves his hold' transfers to the badger the bulldog's own proverbial tenacity. 'Grins' means bares its teeth. Brewer stresses the contrast between the badger's bravery and the crowd's cruelty and cowardice.

title: The crowd: drunkard, women, blackguard
short: The human spectators are drunkards, frightened women and boys, and a laughing 'blackguard': a portrait of mob cruelty.
body: Clare's crowd is drawn in brief types. The drunkard, bitten, swears and staggers; the 'frighted women' remove the boys; the 'blackguard' (a scoundrel, pronounced 'blaggard') laughs and pushes the fight on. Such details show the baiting as communal entertainment across the town while hinting at its degradation. 'Hurries on the fray' means urges the fight forward. None of these figures is named or individualised, in contrast with the closely watched badger.

title: Spelling: 'chace', 'agen', 'bye'
short: Clare's original spellings ('chace', 'agen', 'eer', 'bye') are kept here, as in the 1920 edition.
body: Clare's manuscripts are irregular in spelling and almost unpunctuated; editors from the 1820s onward 'corrected' them, and modern editors (Robinson, Powell) have argued for preserving his forms. 'Chace' was an acceptable older spelling of 'chase', 'agen' records his pronunciation of 'again', and 'where eer' is 'wherever'. The badger's attempt to reach the woods is 'an awkward race' because badgers are built for digging, not running.

title: The death of the badger
short: The badger is kicked and beaten until it lets go of its hold and dies; the poem ends without comment.
body: The final couplet lists three sounds ('cackles, groans') and then death, the bare 'dies' as the last word. 'Leaves his hold' marks the first time the badger lets go, the defeat of its tenacity. 'Starts and grins and drives the crowd agen' in line 38 shows that even apparent death is not final until the last line. Readers debate the effect of Clare's refusal to moralise: for some it intensifies indignation, for others it shows an unsentimental countryman's witness. In the manuscript sequence a further block on a tame badger follows, softening the ending; anthologies like this one end with the death.

title: Form: couplets in sonnet-length blocks
short: Rhymed pentameter couplets, grouped in fourteen-line blocks, with mostly end-stopped lines and piled-up verbs.
body: The poem is written in heroic couplets, but Clare groups them in fourteen-line units, so that each block has the length of a sonnet without the sonnet's rhyme scheme or turn; Perkins accordingly speaks of 'badger sonnets'. Most lines are end-stopped and many begin with 'And' or 'He', a paratactic style that moves forward event by event. Verbs pile up ('drives' is especially frequent), giving the narrative its breathless, relentless pace. The final block in the archive is twelve lines long.
